newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Waterford chief urges ratification of merge.
newsitem.headline: Waterford chief urges ratification of merge.

text.p: Irish dairy group Waterford Foods Plc on Monday urged members to vote in favour of a proposed merger with rival Avonmore Foods Plc at a meeting scheduled for July 25.

"In the rapidly changing commercial environment for the dairy sector of the 1990s, there are major benefits in participating in a larger and stronger business structure," group managing director Matt Walsh told shareholders at an annual meeting.
A proposed merger between Ireland's largest dairy companies was approved when shareholders of both Waterford and Avonmore voted overwhelmingly in favour of the merger at a meeting on July 11.
This must now be ratified at a second meeting on July 25 for the merger to take effect.
If approved, the merger will unite two of Ireland's premier food companies with a joint turnover of 2.5 billion Irish pounds and pre-tax profits of 71.5 million.
This will create the largest dairy company in Britain and Ireland and the fourth largest milk processor in the world.

Analysts said the merged company's milk production would far outstrip the dairy operations of Britain's Northern Foods Plc and Unigate Plc and its cheese production would account for 20 percent of the British market.
This is the second time in six years that Avonmore has attempted to merge with Waterford after a similar attempt in 1991 failed.

Speaking at Monday's annual meeting Walsh called on all Waterford Co-op members to attend the Society's special meeting on Friday July 25 as a 75 percent majority is required if the merger is to proceed, therefore a large attendance is required.
"The proposal to merge Waterford and Avonmore into a new farmer controlled entity offers a compelling business logic and is the ideal strategic response," Walsh said.
He reminded farmers of the weak international dairy markets and high relative milk prices which severely impacted Waterford's 1996 performance.
Waterford's profits and share price plunged with margins squeezed by lower butter and milk prices in 1996, which resulted in the company issuing a profit warning.

"It is essential that milk prices and market returns are kept in balance if the Group stands alone. However, the savings arising from the merger will provide the scope to be a leading payer for milk into the future," Walsh said.

As part of Avonmore's merger proposals farmers trading with the new group will receive a "patronage bonus scheme" which would give milk producers supplying the group a premium of three pence per gallon for their produce.

"The Waterford business will make a highly significant contribution to the enlarged operation through the high quality of our assets and milk pool; range of products, brands and markets; strength of market positions and distribution capabilities," Walsh said.
The two companies have significant synergies with interests in Europe, Britain and America. -- Carmel Linnane, Dublin newsroom + 353 1 676 9775
